lessons.title: The 1991 Balance of Payments Crisis and the Inflation Shock of Liberalization

children.text: In May 1991, boxes of Indian gold were flown out of the country and physically pledged to the Bank of England and a Swiss bank, collateral for emergency loans to keep India from defaulting on its foreign debt. It remains one of the most humbling moments in the country's economic history, and it is also the moment that finally broke the License Raj regime you studied in the last lesson, not through gradual reform, but because the government ran out of any other option.

body.text: The 1991 balance of payments crisis was the forcing function, not a choice. Decades of chronic deficit-driven inflation and a supply side shackled by licensing finally collided with a genuine external emergency, and the government that inherited the crisis dismantled more of the License Raj in a few months than the previous four decades had managed.

body.title: From Crisis to Reform in Twelve Months

events.title: The Gulf War Oil Shock
events.description: Iraq's invasion of Kuwait spikes global oil prices again and disrupts remittances and the evacuation costs of Indian workers in the region, adding fresh strain to an already fragile external position.

events.title: Confidence Collapses
events.description: Political instability, with successive short-lived governments, combines with international credit rating downgrades, making it harder and costlier for India to borrow abroad just as it needed foreign exchange most.

events.title: Reserves Hit Rock Bottom
events.description: India's foreign exchange reserves fall to a level widely cited as barely enough to cover two to three weeks of essential imports, a genuine emergency for a country that cannot pay for its oil and other critical imports.

events.title: Gold Is Pledged Abroad
events.description: As an emergency bridge, India airlifts and pledges gold reserves to the Bank of England and a Swiss bank to raise foreign currency, a move widely reported as deeply symbolic of how dire the situation had become.

events.title: A New Government, A New Direction
events.description: P.V. Narasimha Rao becomes Prime Minister with Dr. Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, and moves immediately to negotiate emergency support and launch structural reform, rather than manage the crisis incrementally.

events.title: Devaluation and Delicensing
events.description: The rupee is devalued in two steps over a few days, and the New Industrial Policy abolishes industrial licensing for most sectors almost overnight, the most direct dismantling of the License Raj framework from the last lesson.

body.label: Gold Pledged as Collateral
body.value: Dozens of tonnes, in more than one tranche
body.context: Gold reserves were physically flown out and pledged to the Bank of England and a Swiss bank in mid-1991 to secure emergency foreign currency, an episode still cited today as a cautionary tale about the cost of running down forex reserves.

children.text: No single event caused this crisis. Years of fiscal deficits, financed partly through external commercial borrowing rather than the RBI's domestic deficit monetization from the last lesson, had steadily built up India's external debt through the 1980s. The 1990 Gulf War oil shock then hit an economy that was already import-dependent on oil and running low on buffers. Political instability made it harder to respond decisively, and international credit downgrades closed off the option of simply borrowing more to buy time. By January 1991, the reserves cushion that would normally absorb a shock like this had essentially run out.

body.text: The gold pledge is worth sitting with. This was not a poor country with no assets, it was a country with real wealth, including centuries of accumulated gold, that had nonetheless mismanaged its external finances badly enough to need emergency collateral just to avoid defaulting on its debt. It remains one of the sharpest illustrations in Indian economic history of why foreign exchange reserves and fiscal discipline are not abstract policy concerns.

children.text: The Reforms: Devaluation, Delicensing, and the IMF

The Rao government's response was unusually fast and unusually sweeping for a country that had spent four decades moving slowly. The rupee was devalued in two steps within days to make exports more competitive and close the external gap. The New Industrial Policy of 1991 abolished industrial licensing for all but a short negative list of industries, dramatically loosened the MRTP Act restrictions on large firms, and opened the door to foreign direct investment in sectors that had been closed for decades. In parallel, India secured emergency financing from the IMF, tied to conditions requiring continued fiscal consolidation and trade liberalization, which gave the government external cover, and external pressure, to keep the reforms going rather than reverse course once the immediate crisis eased.

columns.label: License Raj India (pre-1991)
points: Industrial production required government licenses for most sectors
High tariffs and import licensing sharply restricted foreign trade
Foreign direct investment was heavily restricted or barred outright
Fiscal deficits were routinely financed by the RBI creating money

columns.label: Liberalizing India (post-1991)
points: Industrial licensing abolished for most sectors overnight
Import tariffs and licensing progressively reduced through the 1990s
Foreign direct investment actively courted in most sectors
Deficit financing gradually disciplined, ending automatic monetization by 1997

children.text: The Inflation Shock of Liberalization Itself

It is worth being precise about which engine drove the inflation spike that followed. A currency devaluation is a classic imported cost-push shock: overnight, every rupee of imported oil, machinery, and raw material costs more, and that flows straight through into wholesale and retail prices. WPI inflation is widely cited as running around 13 to 14% through 1991-92, a real, painful cost to households in the short run. But this was structurally different from the chronic inflation of the License Raj era. Once licensing was dismantled, supply could finally respond to demand the way Chapter 1's framework assumes it should, and through the rest of the 1990s, as the reforms bedded in, inflation gradually eased. The crisis inflicted a sharp, one-time cost-push shock in exchange for retiring a chronic, decades-long structural one, arguably the best trade India's economy ever made under duress.

body.title: One-Time Shock or Repeating Regime?
body.scenario: A retail investor in late 1991 sees WPI inflation running above 13% and panics, assuming India is about to repeat the chronic high-inflation pattern of the 1970s and 1980s covered in the last lesson.
body.prompt: Using the distinction between a headline print and the underlying regime from Chapter 1, explain why this investor's panic may be based on a misread. What would you actually want to check before concluding whether this is a one-time transition cost or a return to a chronic regime?
body.modelAnswer: The 1991 inflation spike has a clear, identifiable, one-time cause, the devaluation's direct pass-through into import costs, rather than an ongoing structural driver like License Raj-era deficit monetization or licensing-constrained supply. To judge whether it is transitory or a new chronic regime, the investor should watch whether inflation eases as the devaluation's one-time effect works through the base (the base effect from Chapter 1 again), whether the fiscal deficit is actually being brought under control as promised under the IMF programme, and whether supply-side reforms are genuinely letting businesses expand output. Through the 1990s, all three of these improved, which is exactly why the 1991 spike proved to be a transition cost rather than a repeat of the previous three decades.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What was the most direct link between the July 1991 rupee devaluation and the inflation spike that followed?
options: The devaluation directly raised the price of imported goods and inputs, a classic cost-push transmission
The devaluation increased India's money supply overnight
The devaluation caused a sudden nationwide drought
The devaluation abolished the RBI's control over interest rates
body.explanation: A devaluation makes foreign currency more expensive in rupee terms, so anything imported, oil, machinery, raw materials, costs more immediately. That is a textbook cost-push mechanism, distinct from the demand-pull or chronic monetary dynamics covered in earlier lessons.

points: The 1991 balance of payments crisis was the forcing function that ended the License Raj: reserves fell to barely weeks of import cover, and gold was pledged abroad as emergency collateral.
The July 1991 rupee devaluation and the New Industrial Policy dismantled decades of industrial licensing and import restrictions within months, not years.

The inflation spike that followed, WPI running around 13-14% in 1991-92, was primarily an imported cost-push shock from the devaluation, structurally different from the chronic, licensing-driven inflation of the previous era.
Unlike the License Raj years, this shock proved transitory: once supply could finally respond to demand, inflation eased through the rest of the 1990s.
This sets up the next lesson directly: how India moved from crisis-driven reform to a formal, RBI-led inflation-targeting framework by the 2010s.
